question.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{\text{d}u}{2}.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & ={\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3/2}}{3} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$
